summary: The note is an overview of sous-vide cooking, a French technique of cooking vacuum-sealed food in a precisely controlled low-temperature water bath. It traces the method from Georges Pralus's 1974 foie gras work through its adoption by chefs, its spread worldwide, the arrival of affordable home equipment and smart-device technology, and its use in education and sustainability debates. It cites dated events and studies, such as a 2027 study on vitamin retention, and closes on the technique's future potential.
one_line: Overview of sous-vide cooking's history, science, global spread, home equipment, nutrition, education and sustainability, from Pralus's 1974 foie gras to modern smart devices.
key_facts: Sous-vide translates to "under vacuum" and involves sealing food in an airtight plastic bag or glass jar and cooking it in a precisely controlled, low-temperature water bath.
Chef Georges Pralus first applied sous-vide to foie gras in 1974 in the kitchens of Troisgros in Roanne, France, improving texture and flavor and reducing product wastage.
The note says the roots of water-bath cooking principles go back to the enlightenment era, but the modern form took shape in the mid-20th century.
In October 2024, Michelin-starred chef Thomas Keller published a sous-vide compendium that helped raise interest among chefs and home cooks worldwide.

On November 15, 2024, Dr. Bruno Goussault, called the father of modern sous-vide, lectured at the International Culinary Technology Conference in Berlin on how consistent temperature cooks food evenly without overcooking.
On December 1, 2025, Chef Isla Ford demonstrated sous-vide with proteins, vegetables, fruits and legumes at the "SousVide Down Under" food festival in Sydney, Australia.

Companies such as Anova and Joule introduced affordable, compact immersion circulators; by September 2026 the devices were household names, and Rachel Nguyen's "Sous-Vide Secrets" workshops in Chicago were overbooked.
At the Silicon Valley Food Tech Summit in February 2027, innovators showcased sous-vide devices that could be voice-controlled via smart home systems.
On May 9, 2027, food scientist Maria Vazquez published a study finding sous-vide cooked vegetables retained 90% of their vitamins versus 55% for boiling.
On August 2, 2028, Executive Chef William Harper told a lecture at the Culinary Institute of America that understanding sous-vide is an essential skill for any modern chef.
The London Green Food Conference on March 11, 2029 held a panel on sous-vide energy efficiency, stating precise temperature and time mean less water and electricity use than conventional cooking.
Early sous-vide equipment was bulky and expensive, and later miniaturization and Bluetooth-enabled, smartphone-controlled devices made it accessible to home cooks.
